--- title: "Visualizing ML & NLP Models" subtitle: "Week 13 · What a model does, beyond its accuracy" author: "DATS 6401 — Visualization of Complex Data · Junjun Yin" format: revealjs --- ## Today's session {.smaller} | | | | |---|---|---| | **Block 1** | Concepts & Theory — *this deck* | ~45 min | | **Block 2** | Guided demo: a tumor classifier, a review classifier, clustering, then the live loop | ~70 min | | ☕ | Break | ~15 min | | **Block 4** | Wrap-up & homework preview | ~10 min | | **Block 3** | Hands-on: choose a threshold, then connect your client to your server — **on your own after class** | ~45 min | ::: {.gw-box} In Week 11 you wrote a client, and in Week 12 a server that wraps a model. Today you look inside a model: how it fails, what it uses, and how sure it is. Then you connect the three parts into one system. ::: # Accuracy is where the questions start {background-color="#00223e"} ## One number, six patients The model for most of today predicts whether a breast tumor is malignant or benign, from measurements of a biopsy image. The next two slides describe the data and the model. On 143 tumors it has never seen, the model is **95.8% accurate**. That means it called 6 of them wrong. The accuracy does not say which 6, or anything else we need in order to use the model. Three questions are left open, and each one has a chart: 1. **How does it fail?** Which errors it makes, and what they cost. 2. **What is it using?** Which measurements drive the predictions. 3. **How sure is it?** Whether its confidence tells us anything. ## The data: one row per tumor | diagnosis | mean radius | mean texture | mean area | worst radius | worst area | |:------------|--------------:|---------------:|------------:|---------------:|-------------:| | malignant | 18 | 10.4 | 1001 | 25.4 | 2019 | | malignant | 20.6 | 17.8 | 1326 | 25 | 1956 | | benign | 13.5 | 14.4 | 566.3 | 15.1 | 711.2 | | benign | 13.1 | 15.7 | 520 | 14.5 | 630.5 | Four of the 569 rows and 5 of the 30 columns. Each column summarizes the cell nuclei in one biopsy image. The model should predict `diagnosis`. ```python from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True) # ships with scikit-learn X, y = bc.data, bc.target # y: 0 = malignant, 1 = benign ``` ## The model: a random forest A **decision tree** asks a series of yes-or-no questions about the measurements, such as "is the worst radius above 16.8?", and ends at a diagnosis. A **random forest** trains many trees, each on a different random sample of the tumors, and lets them vote. The share of trees that vote malignant is the model's probability that the tumor is malignant. That probability is what the rest of today builds on. ## The code: train on some tumors, test on the rest ```python from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split # Hold back a quarter of the tumors. The model never sees them. X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y) model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, random_state=42) model.fit(X_train, y_train) # learn from 426 tumors model.score(X_test, y_test) # accuracy on the other 143: 0.958 ``` We judge the model only on the 143 held-back tumors. A model can memorize the tumors it trained on, so its score on those says little. # How does it fail? {background-color="#00223e"} ## Four kinds of outcome {.smaller} ::: {#0a371f62 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=868 height=369 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: "Positive" means the thing we are looking for, which here is malignant. Every tumor in the test set lands in one of these four cells. - **Recall** reads across the top row: of the tumors that are malignant, what share did the model catch? TP / (TP + FN) - **Precision** reads down the left column: of the tumors the model called malignant, what share are? TP / (TP + FP) ## The confusion matrix ::: {#91398187 .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=422 height=379 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Read it by row. Of 53 malignant tumors, the model called 49 malignant and 4 benign. Of 90 benign tumors, it called 88 benign and 2 malignant. ## The code: a confusion matrix ```python from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator( model, X_test, y_test, display_labels=["malignant", "benign"], # names for classes 0 and 1 cmap="Blues") ``` One call draws the chart on the previous slide. For the numbers: ```python from sklearn.metrics import classification_report print(classification_report(y_test, model.predict(X_test), target_names=["malignant", "benign"])) ``` ```text precision recall f1-score support malignant 0.961 0.925 0.942 53 benign 0.957 0.978 0.967 90 ``` ## The two errors do not cost the same {.smaller} A benign tumor called malignant leads to more tests. A malignant tumor called benign is a cancer that goes untreated. Accuracy counts both as one error each. The metrics below keep them apart. | Metric | Question it answers | Here | |---|---|---| | Accuracy | Of all tumors, how many were called correctly? | 137 / 143 = **0.958** | | Recall (malignant) | Of the real cancers, how many did the model catch? | 49 / 53 = **0.925** | | Precision (malignant) | Of the tumors it called malignant, how many were? | 49 / 51 = **0.961** | ::: {.gw-box} Which metric matters depends on which error is worse. For screening, a missed cancer is the worse error, so recall is the number to report first. ::: ## How to read an ROC curve {.smaller} ::: {#ac2a77e5 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=637 height=389 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ROC stands for **receiver operating characteristic**. The curve plots recall against the false alarm rate, one point for each threshold. Moving right along a curve means lowering the threshold: the model catches more cancers and also raises more false alarms. A curve that climbs steeply toward the top-left corner catches most cancers before it raises many false alarms. The diagonal is what guessing would give. ## The threshold is a choice ::: {#bd581c40 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=940 height=360 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The model outputs a probability. The label comes from a cutoff, and 0.5 is only the default. Each point on the ROC curve is one possible cutoff. ## The code: probabilities and thresholds ```python # Ask for probabilities instead of labels. Column 0 is P(malignant). p_malignant = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 0] is_malignant = (y_test == 0) from sklearn.metrics import RocCurveDisplay RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(is_malignant, p_malignant) ``` `predict` gives a label. `predict_proba` gives the probability behind it, so we can apply any threshold ourselves: ```python for t in [0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]: called = p_malignant >= t # called malignant missed = (is_malignant & ~called).sum() # cancers not called alarms = (~is_malignant & called).sum() # healthy, but called print(t, missed, alarms) ``` ## What each threshold does to these 143 patients {.smaller} | Call it malignant when P(malignant) is at least | Missed cancers | False alarms | |---|---|---| | 0.5 (the default) | 4 | 2 | | 0.4 | 3 | 3 | | 0.3 | 1 | 7 | | 0.2 | **0** | 9 | | 0.1 | 0 | 20 | Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 finds all four missed cancers and sends seven more healthy patients for further tests. ::: {.gw-box} Choosing the threshold is not a modeling decision. It depends on what each error costs, and the people who know those costs are usually not the ones who trained the model. This table and the chart before it are how they take part in the choice. ::: # What is it using? {background-color="#00223e"} ## Feature importance ::: {#70acf730 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=771 height=369 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: A sorted bar chart, so the values are compared on a common scale. The top of the list is three size measurements: area, perimeter and radius. ## The code: feature importance, two ways ```python # 1. What the forest split on. Training already computed it. importance = pd.Series(model.feature_importances_, index=X.columns) importance.sort_values().tail(10).plot.barh(color="steelblue") ``` Sorting before plotting is what makes the chart readable. ```python from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance # 2. What the model cannot do without: shuffle one column # at a time and measure how much accuracy is lost. perm = permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=30, random_state=0) perm.importances_mean # one number per feature ``` The second re-scores the model many times, on the test set. It is the one to trust when features overlap. ## Correlated features share the credit {.smaller} ::: {#c4aaab2f .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=810 height=348 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Area, perimeter and radius describe the same nucleus, and their correlations are 0.98 to 0.99. The forest divides the credit among them. Shuffling any one of them barely changes the accuracy, because the other two still carry the information. Both charts are correct. They answer different questions, so a feature importance chart should say which definition it uses. # Where does it fail, and does it know? {background-color="#00223e"} ## The error map ::: {#4e8c40e2 .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-10-output-1.png){width=696 height=388 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The projection is PCA, the method from Week 7. The six errors are not scattered. They lie where the two classes meet, among tumors that resemble both. ## The code: the error map ```python from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.decomposition import PCA # Put all 30 measurements on one scale, then find the 2 directions # that spread the data most. Both are fitted on the training tumors. scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train) pca = PCA(n_components=2).fit(scaler.transform(X_train)) pcs = pca.transform(scaler.transform(X_test)) # test tumors, in 2-D wrong = model.predict(X_test) != y_test # True for the 6 errors plt.scatter(pcs[~wrong, 0], pcs[~wrong, 1], c=y_test[~wrong], s=22) plt.scatter(pcs[wrong, 0], pcs[wrong, 1], marker="x", color="black") ``` Scaling comes first because area is in the hundreds and smoothness is below 1. Without it, PCA would see only the large columns. ## Confidence carries information ::: {#9bd7551f .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-11-output-1.png){width=715 height=341 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: For most tumors the model answers close to 0 or close to 1. For the six it got wrong, it answered between 0.29 and 0.76. The probability tells us which predictions to trust less. This is the reason the Week 12 server returns the probabilities and not only the label. # The same questions for a text model {background-color="#00223e"} ## A review classifier {.smaller} ::: {#fb7d7b0e .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=354 height=321 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The data is IMDB movie reviews, each labeled positive or negative. TF-IDF turns a review into word weights, as in Week 7, and logistic regression learns one coefficient per word. The model is trained on 20,000 reviews. **How does it fail?** It gets 141 of 1,000 wrong: 71 negative reviews called positive, and 70 positive reviews called negative. Here the two errors cost the same, and the matrix shows the model does not favor either class. ## From a review to a row of numbers {.smaller} > "Its the best movie I have seen in 2000, it has the beautiful and talented > Natalie Portman in it. It has a great storyline, cast and soundtrack. I enjoyed > it very much. 10 out of 10" ::: {#e29edc49 .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-13-output-1.png){width=714 height=302 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: A model cannot take text as input. The vectorizer keeps the 5,000 most common words and gives every review one number per word. This review uses 12 of them, so its row holds 12 values and 4,988 zeros. A word scores higher when it is rare in other reviews. The order of the words is not kept. ## The code: a text classifier ```python from datasets import load_dataset from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression imdb = load_dataset("imdb") # downloads once, then reads a local copy train = pd.DataFrame(imdb["train"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(20000))) test = pd.DataFrame(imdb["test"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(1000))) text_model = make_pipeline( TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", max_features=5000), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42), ).fit(train["text"], train["label"]) text_model.score(test["text"], test["label"]) # 0.859 ``` Each row is one review and a label, 0 for negative or 1 for positive. The pipeline turns text into 5,000 word weights, then into P(positive). ## A word cloud looks good and shows little ::: {#ee3cfd38 .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-14-output-1.png){width=1041 height=342 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The largest words in both clouds are "movie", "film" and "one". Size shows how often a word appears, and the most frequent words are the same in praise and in complaint. The words that separate the two classes are on the next slide. ## What it uses: one coefficient per word ::: {#ed52fe6d .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-15-output-1.png){width=714 height=398 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The model has learned which words signal praise and which signal complaint. It adds up word weights. It does not read sentences. ## Explaining one prediction {.smaller} ::: {#fc55f8ee .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

While I thought this was a good film about JFK Jr it was a little hard to follow the timeline. It jumped around quite a bit without ever mentioning what year they were in. Otherwise not great acting, and not really a great film, but it was nice to learn a little more about who JFK Jr was.

``` ::: ::: ::: {#cc0b2229 .cell execution_count=16} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-17-output-1.png){width=790 height=322 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: A **positive** review, and the model says P(positive) = **0.95**. The largest push comes from "great", which the writer used in "not great acting" and "not really a great film". The answer is right and part of the reason is wrong. ## The code: word weights and one prediction ```python vectorizer = text_model.named_steps["tfidfvectorizer"] classifier = text_model.named_steps["logisticregression"] # One coefficient per word: below zero pushes toward negative words = pd.Series(classifier.coef_[0], index=vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()).sort_values() pd.concat([words.head(10), words.tail(10)]).plot.barh() ``` For one review, a word's contribution is its value in that review times its coefficient: ```python row = vectorizer.transform([test["text"][743]]).toarray()[0] # 5,000 numbers contribution = pd.Series(row * classifier.coef_[0], index=vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()) contribution[row > 0].sort_values().plot.barh() # only the words it uses ``` ## Read the errors {.smaller} The quickest way to understand a text model is to read the cases it got wrong while it was most sure. > "This is, without a doubt, the most hilarious movie I've ever seen. Seriously, > if the makers of this movie are ever discovered, they'll put guys like Jim > Carrey out of a job." A **negative** review. The model said P(positive) = **0.86**. The writer is being sarcastic, and every weighted word in the review is a word of praise. > "Great cult flick for MST-3K types: Richard Boone is a mess -- bad hair, > arthritis ... about as good as a bad dino-flick can get" A **positive** review. The model said P(positive) = **0.18**. The writer enjoys the film for being bad, and the model counts "bad" twice. No metric would have shown this. Reading a few confident errors is the text version of the error map. ## The code: finding the confident errors ```python p = text_model.predict_proba(test["text"])[:, 1] # P(positive) results = test.assign(p_positive=p) results["wrong"] = (p >= 0.5).astype(int) != results["label"] results["sureness"] = abs(p - 0.5) # distance from 0.5 # The errors the model was most sure about worst = results[results["wrong"]].sort_values("sureness").tail(3) for _, r in worst.iterrows(): print(r["label"], round(r["p_positive"], 2), r["text"][:300]) ``` Sorting by sureness puts the most useful reviews at the end. Read them before you look at any more metrics. ## Errors are concentrated where the model is unsure ::: {#2282a1e6 .cell execution_count=17} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-18-output-1.png){width=715 height=331 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The model answers between 0.35 and 0.65 for 22% of the reviews. Those reviews account for 55% of its errors. An app that uses this model can treat that band differently, for example by labeling the review "mixed" or by sending it to a person. ## What word counts cannot see | Sentence | P(positive) | |---|---:| | This movie is good. | 0.81 | | This movie is not good. | 0.81 | | It was boring. | 0.01 | | It was never boring. | 0.01 | The model gives each pair the same score. It weighs every word on its own, so it cannot connect "not" to "good". In this model the cause is even simpler. "Not" and "never" are on the list of stop words that the vectorizer removes, so the model never receives them. ## A model that reads the sentence {.smaller} **DistilBERT** is a small transformer. Other people have already trained it on sentences from movie reviews, so we download it and use it without training. It reads the words in order, and each word is interpreted with the words around it. | | Word counts | DistilBERT | |------------------------------------------------|--------:|--------:| | This movie is good. | 0.81 | 1.00 | | This movie is not good. | 0.81 | 0.00 | | It was boring. | 0.01 | 0.00 | | It was never boring. | 0.01 | 1.00 | | A sarcastic negative review: "the most hilarious movie I've ever seen" | 0.86 | 1.00 | | **Accuracy on the same 1,000 reviews** | **0.859** | **0.879** | The numbers are P(positive). DistilBERT handles "not" and "never". The sarcastic review still fools it, and it is more sure of the wrong answer than the word-count model was. ## The code: a pretrained text model ```python from transformers import pipeline # Downloads the model once, about 270 MB. Then it runs on your laptop. reader = pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english") reader(["This movie is good.", "This movie is not good."]) ``` ``` [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.9999}, {'label': 'NEGATIVE', 'score': 0.9998}] ``` This is the Hugging Face library from the Week 12 detection server. The model reads at most 512 tokens, so for long reviews call `reader(texts, truncation=True)`. ## Inside the model: where it places each review {.smaller} ::: {#e6fbc2dd .cell execution_count=20} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-21-output-1.png){width=1089 height=379 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Before it answers, the model turns each review into 768 numbers. UMAP, from Week 7, draws those numbers in two dimensions. The model puts reviews in two groups, and its errors are reviews placed in the wrong group. The model answers above 0.95 or below 0.05 for 90% of the reviews, and 78 of its 121 errors are among those. It is more accurate than the word-count model, and its confidence tells you less. # Structure without labels {background-color="#00223e"} ## K-means and DBSCAN make different assumptions {.smaller} ::: {#f98b0e58 .cell execution_count=21} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-22-output-1.png){width=906 height=292 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: When the data has no labels, the question is whether it has groups. - **K-means** assumes round groups, and you tell it how many to find. - **DBSCAN** finds groups as regions where points are packed closely. It decides the number itself, and it marks isolated points as noise. HDBSCAN, which BERTopic used in Week 7, is DBSCAN without a fixed radius. ## DBSCAN on locations ::: {#eddb4ecd .cell execution_count=22} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-23-output-1.png){width=888 height=398 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: DBSCAN finds 49 clusters and labels 1,041 sites as noise. The clusters are metropolitan areas: New York and New Jersey (297 sites), the Bay Area (170), Los Angeles (152). The gray sites are the highway network between them. ## The code: DBSCAN on coordinates ```python from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN sites = pd.read_csv("data/superchargers_us.csv") # lat and lon per site EARTH_RADIUS_KM = 6371.0088 eps_km = 25 # how close counts as a neighbor sites["cluster"] = DBSCAN( eps=eps_km / EARTH_RADIUS_KM, # kilometers, converted to radians min_samples=5, # at least 5 sites in that radius metric="haversine", # distance over the Earth's surface algorithm="ball_tree", ).fit_predict(np.radians(sites[["lat", "lon"]])) ``` Latitude and longitude are angles, so straight-line distance is wrong for them. DBSCAN returns one number per site: its cluster, or **-1** for noise. The map is a scatter plot colored by that number. ## The parameters are part of the result {.smaller} The same 2,254 sites, with the neighborhood radius changed and nothing else: | Radius | Clusters | Sites labeled noise | Largest cluster | |---|---|---|---| | 10 km | 41 | 1,738 | 116 | | 25 km | 49 | 1,041 | 297 | | 50 km | 50 | 607 | 424 | | 100 km | 20 | 188 | 1,093 | At 100 km most of the eastern United States, from Florida to Massachusetts, becomes one cluster. ::: {.gw-box} There is no correct radius to discover. A cluster map should state its parameters, for the same reason a histogram should state its bin width. ::: # From the model to the user {background-color="#00223e"} ## Showing uncertainty in the client {.smaller} A user never sees the confusion matrix. They see one prediction, in an app. What the app shows decides whether they can tell a sure answer from an unsure one. - **Label only.** A 0.99 and a 0.53 look identical. - **Label and its probability.** Better, but for three or more classes it hides how close the second choice was. - **The full distribution.** One bar per class. This is what the Week 12 server returns, and it is the display to prefer. For the iris flower `(6.0, 2.7, 5.0, 1.7)`, the Week 12 server answers virginica at 0.53, with versicolor at 0.47. In Block 3 you will send it a flower that comes back at exactly 0.50 and 0.50, and decide what the app should show. ## The code: asking the server ```python import requests flower = {"sepal_length": 6.0, "sepal_width": 2.7, "petal_length": 5.0, "petal_width": 1.7} try: r = requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict", json=flower, timeout=5) r.raise_for_status() out = r.json() except requests.RequestException as e: print("Could not reach the server:", e) ``` The Week 11 pattern: a timeout, a status check, a handled failure. The answer: ```json {"prediction": "virginica", "confidence": 0.53, "probabilities": {"setosa": 0.0, "versicolor": 0.47, "virginica": 0.53}} ``` In Streamlit, `st.bar_chart(pd.Series(out["probabilities"]))` draws it. ## One system, three parts ```text Terminal 1 your Week 12 server uvicorn server_skeleton:app --reload Terminal 2 the Streamlit client streamlit run app_live_predictions.py Browser sliders in, prediction and full distribution out ``` The client holds no model. Each prediction is a request to the server and a response back, which is the loop from Week 11. In the demo we stop the server while the app is open. The client should report that the server is unreachable and keep running. Your final project has this shape, with your own model in the server. ## Discussion {.gw-discussion} **1.** For the tumor model, who should choose the threshold? What would you show them so that they can? **2.** The review classifier is wrong about sarcasm. Which of today's charts would have revealed that, and which would not? **3.** Your final project puts a model in front of a user. What will your app show when the model is unsure? ## Coming up next — Block 2 {.smaller} A live demo, with the notebook provided: 1. **The tumor classifier:** confusion matrix, recall and precision, the ROC curve, and the threshold table 2. **What it uses and where it fails:** two kinds of feature importance, the error map, and the confidence histogram 3. **The review classifier:** the same three questions, and reading the confident errors 4. **Clustering:** K-means and DBSCAN, then Supercharger sites on a map 5. **The live loop:** your Week 12 server, the notebook as a client, then the Streamlit app **Then Block 3:** choose a threshold for the tumor model and defend it, then connect your client to your Week 12 server. **Readings:** scikit-learn visualization API · scikit-learn on permutation importance · Wilke, ch. 16 **Homework preview:** two visuals that explain a model, a working client and server, and a short account of where your model is weak.
